text: Cleo had invited her new colleagues for dinner and spent the afternoon on an elaborate fish dish. When she lifted the lid, the kitchen filled with smoke and the smell of scorched skin. The guests laughed kindly and opened the windows. One of them suggested ordering pizza. Cleo stood by the stove with the ruined pan and felt her whole face go hot, her ears ringing. She had bragged about her cooking all week at the office. Now they would all know. She wanted to sink through the floor, to be anywhere else. She kept her back to the room far longer than she needed, scraping at nothing.

At the family barbecue Gus's uncle picked up the burger Gus had grilled, bit into it, and spat it out: raw in the middle. Everyone turned to look. His cousins snickered, and someone took a photo. Gus stood holding the spatula while his face burned and his neck prickled. He was thirty-four and still could not grill a burger in front of his family. He wanted to shrink down into his shoes. He laughed along, too loudly, and kept his eyes on the grill, and for the rest of the afternoon he could not look at anyone without feeling them remember.

On the packed morning train Esme's stomach made a long, loud gurgle in a moment of total silence. A teenager snorted. A man in a suit glanced over at her and away. Esme stared straight ahead at the map above the door while heat crawled up from her collar to her hairline. She felt as if every person in the carriage were looking at her, though most were not. She held her bag tight against her middle and counted the stops. When the doors finally opened at her station she was the first one out, walking fast, head down, not looking back.

Bram ran for the bus, waving, and slipped on the wet pavement just as he reached the doors, landing flat on his back in a puddle in front of the whole queue. Someone clapped. He got up with his trousers soaked and his bag spilled open, papers everywhere, and picked them up one by one while the passengers watched through the windows. His face was scalding. He could not bring himself to get on that bus. He stood at the stop pretending to check his phone until it pulled away, and then walked the whole way to work in wet clothes.

Ines's mother called on speaker while Ines was in a meeting, and before she could mute it the whole room heard her mother ask whether she had remembered her rash cream. There was a silence, then someone coughed. Ines fumbled with the phone, her fingers suddenly thick and clumsy. Her face burned. She said she would call back and hung up, and the manager went on with the slide as if nothing had happened, which made it worse. For the rest of the meeting Ines stared at her notepad, drawing small boxes, unable to lift her eyes to anyone.

Kai's brother called him at the office and, laughing, read out the poem Kai had written at fifteen for a girl in his class, found in a box at their parents' house. Kai had left the call on speaker by mistake. Two colleagues at nearby desks went quiet and then grinned at each other. Kai grabbed the phone and turned the speaker off, but it was too late. His ears were burning. He wanted the floor to open. For the rest of the day, every time someone laughed near him, he was sure it was about the poem, and he kept his head bent low over his keyboard.

Halfway through her presentation to the board, Pia saw that she had been clicking through last year's slides. The numbers were all wrong. The chief executive raised an eyebrow and asked, drily, if they had traveled back in time. A few people chuckled. Pia's mouth went dry and her face flooded with heat. She stood at the front of the room with the remote in her hand, every eye on her, and could not find the right file. Her hands shook as she searched. She felt small and exposed, like a child caught out in class, and she could not look at anyone.

Milo sent a message complaining about his manager to what he thought was a friend. It went to the whole team channel instead. By the time he saw it, fourteen people had read it, including the manager. Milo sat frozen at his desk, the blood draining from his face and then rushing back, hot. He deleted it, but everyone had seen. When the manager walked past, Milo stared at his screen, his shoulders hunched up around his ears. He wanted to disappear. At lunch he ate in his car so he would not have to face anyone in the kitchen.

Lale entered her giant marrow in the village show, bragging to everyone for weeks that it would win. On the morning of judging, she lifted the cloth to find it had split open and gone soft overnight, its insides spilling onto the table. People gathered to look. A child asked what the smell was. Lale stood beside it while her neighbors murmured, her face burning, her hands hanging useless at her sides. She could hear her own boasting echoing in her head. She wanted to scoop the whole thing up and run home and never show her face at the show again.

Oren's neighbors leaned over the fence to watch as he tried to start his new mower, pulling the cord again and again with a flourish while it sputtered. On the eighth pull he fell backwards into the flower bed. The neighbors burst out laughing. One filmed it. Oren picked himself up, soil on his shirt, and felt his whole face go hot and tight. He could not look at the fence. He wheeled the mower back into the shed and stayed inside it for a while, in the dim light, among the rakes, until he heard them go indoors.

In the crowded clinic waiting room the receptionist called out Rafa's name, and then, loudly, the reason for his appointment. A few people looked up. A woman smirked behind her magazine. Rafa stood and walked to the desk, his neck and ears prickling with heat, his eyes fixed on the floor. It felt as if the whole room now knew the most private thing about him. When he sat back down he held a leaflet up in front of his face and pretended to read it, willing the minutes to pass, and did not look up again until he was called.

The nurse asked Una to step on the scale and read the number out loud, in front of the open door where other patients were passing. Una stood there in her socks while the nurse wrote it down and said, cheerfully, that they should talk about her diet. Una felt her face go hot and her stomach tighten. A man in the corridor glanced in. She wanted to pull her coat around her and vanish. She stepped down and sat on the paper-covered bed with her arms crossed over herself, staring at a poster about hand washing, unable to meet the nurse's eyes.

The postman handed Femi a parcel with the name of an adult shop printed in large letters across the side, just as his mother-in-law came up the path behind him. She looked at the box and then at him. Femi felt the blood rush to his face. He tucked the parcel under his arm, label inward, and said something about a mistake, a wrong address, and heard how thin it sounded. His ears were on fire. All through lunch he could feel her glancing at him across the table, and he could not taste anything he ate.

A letter came from the school: Noor's application to teach there had been rejected, and the head had written, in a line meant to be kind, that her spelling in the cover letter had been noted. Noor read it standing in the hallway. She had written that letter three times. She looked at her copy and saw the mistake at once, in the very first line: the school's own name, spelled wrong. Her face went hot and her stomach turned. She pictured them passing it around the staff room. She shoved the letter in a drawer and could not bring herself to look at it again.

Zola's dog, which she had told the whole park was perfectly trained, ran off during the dog show, jumped into the pond, and then shook muddy water all over the judge. The crowd roared. Zola ran after him calling his name, her face burning, her voice getting higher and higher while he ignored her completely. When she finally caught his collar, dripping and panting, everyone was watching. She dragged him away without looking back. On the walk home she kept her head down and took the long way, so she would not pass anyone from the park.

Jun had taught his parrot a few rude words as a joke years ago and forgotten about it. When his new partner's parents came for dinner, the bird chose that moment, in a quiet pause, to repeat them loudly, twice. The mother put down her fork. Jun's face flooded with heat. He mumbled something and covered the cage with a towel, and the bird went on muttering underneath it. For the rest of the meal Jun kept his eyes on his plate, wanting to shrink into his chair, every clink of cutlery sounding too loud in the silence.

Movers carried Hana's belongings into the new building while the neighbors watched from the landing, and a box split open on the stairs, spilling out her old diaries, a stack of unpaid bills and a tangle of worn underwear. A neighbor's teenager giggled. Hana dropped to her knees on the stairs, scooping everything back in with both arms, her face on fire. She could not look up. It felt as though her whole private life lay open on the steps for strangers to read. For weeks afterward she took the lift early in the morning so she would not meet them.

At the housewarming party in his new flat, Teo showed his friends the shelves he had built himself. As he leaned on one to demonstrate, it tore out of the wall and dumped every book onto the floor. His friends went silent, and then someone laughed. Teo stood among the scattered books, his face burning, his hands suddenly with nowhere to go. He had talked about those shelves for a month. He knelt to pick up the books, taking far longer than he needed, because he could not stand up and face the room.

Wren had told her cycling club she was ready for the long hill ride. Twenty minutes up the first climb, she had to get off and push, red-faced and gasping, while the whole group waited at the top watching her walk the bicycle up. Nobody said anything. That was worse. Her legs were shaking and her face was hot with more than effort. When she reached them she mumbled that her chain was slipping, and saw that no one believed it. For the rest of the ride she stayed at the very back, where no one had to look at her.

Amir wobbled at a red light in front of a cafe full of people, fell sideways slowly with his feet still clipped to the pedals, and lay on the road with the bicycle on top of him. A table of students applauded. He unclipped, stood, and brushed off his knees, his face burning, his ears ringing. He could not look toward the window. He got back on and rode away far too fast, and did not slow down until he was two streets away, where he stopped and stood with his forehead against the cool wall of a building.

At the market checkout Vera's card was declined, twice, with a loud beep each time. The queue behind her grew. The cashier said, not quietly, that she could put some items back. Vera felt her face drain and then burn. She began taking things out of the bag, the cheese, the wine, her hands clumsy, while people shifted and sighed behind her. She could feel their eyes on the back of her neck. She paid for the bread and eggs with coins from the bottom of her purse, and walked out without looking at anyone, wanting to be invisible.

At the busy fish stall Eli haggled loudly, sure of himself, for a whole minute before the seller pointed out, patiently, that the price he was arguing about was per fish, not per kilo, and was already the cheapest in the market. People nearby grinned at each other. Eli felt the heat climb up his neck into his face. He had been so certain. He paid quickly, mumbling, and took the parcel without meeting the seller's eye. All the way home he replayed his own loud voice, and each time his face went hot again.

Stuck indoors on a rainy afternoon, Dara joined a video call to sing for her online choir, not knowing her camera showed the unmade bed and the pile of laundry behind her, or that her flatmate would walk through in a towel. Forty faces saw it all. Someone typed a row of laughing faces in the chat. Dara slammed the laptop shut. Her whole body felt hot and prickly. She sat on the edge of the bed with her hands over her face, listening to the rain, unable to picture showing up at the next rehearsal and meeting every face in it.

On a rainy afternoon Sami's teenage daughter found his old poetry notebook in the attic and read the worst poem aloud to her friends in the living room, doing a dramatic voice. They howled with laughter. Sami walked in in the middle of it. The girls went quiet and stared at him. His face burned; he could feel it all the way to his scalp. He wanted to take the notebook and throw it on the fire, and burn the memory of every line. He managed a weak smile, took the notebook, and went upstairs, where he sat on the bed with the door closed.

Nell's friend came to visit, and Nell, trying to seem well read, talked at length about a novel she had not read. Her friend listened, then gently mentioned that she had written her thesis on it and that the ending Nell described was from the film, not the book. Nell's face went hot. She laughed, too high. Her friend changed the subject kindly, which somehow made it worse. For the rest of the visit Nell could hardly speak, and every time the conversation paused she replayed her own confident voice and felt herself shrink.

Ivo had bragged to his visiting friend about how well he spoke the language here, and when they went out for dinner he ordered confidently in a long speech. The waiter looked puzzled and answered slowly, in the plain words kept for tourists. His friend bit her lip. Ivo felt his face go hot. The waiter, trying to help, repeated back what Ivo had actually ordered, which was, it seemed, a plate of shoes. The next table laughed. Ivo stared at the tablecloth for the rest of the evening, his ears burning, barely touching his food.

Rhea pulled up outside her new job in her ancient car, and as she parked it backfired with a bang that made everyone in the courtyard duck. Then it would not stop smoking. Her new colleagues gathered at the windows. Rhea sat behind the wheel with the smoke curling past, her face burning, gripping the keys. She had told them in the interview that she was very organized, very reliable. She got out, head down, and walked into the building while the engine ticked and hissed behind her, and felt their eyes on her all the way to her desk.

At the car wash Tavi forgot to close the sunroof. Soapy water poured in over his head, and he sat there spluttering while the brushes went on turning and the queue of drivers behind him watched through their windscreens. When the machine finally stopped, he drove out dripping, his shirt soaked, suds on his head. The attendant was laughing so hard he had to lean on the wall. Tavi's face went hot as an oven. He drove straight out onto the road without stopping for the dryer, and did not look in the mirror.

At pickup, Bea's son ran to her across the playground shouting about the family secret he had shared at news time: that his mother snored so loudly his father slept on the sofa. The other parents turned around. Several were smiling. The teacher gave Bea a little wave from the door. Bea felt her face go hot and her throat tighten. She took her son's hand and walked quickly to the car, head down, not answering his chatter. For weeks afterward she dropped him at the gate and left without speaking to anyone.

Quin arrived at the school gate in his pajama bottoms and slippers, having rushed out without thinking, and only noticed when another father glanced down and smiled. Then a group of mothers noticed too. Quin's face went burning hot. His son came running out, looked at the slippers, and said loudly, why are you wearing those. Quin wanted to dissolve into the pavement. He hurried his son to the car, hunched over, and drove home as fast as he could, his ears glowing, going over and over the sight of those smiling faces.

At the crowded beach Yara ran into the sea with a whoop, and a wave pulled the top of her swimsuit clean off. She crouched in the water up to her neck while it drifted away, and a man on a paddleboard fished it out and paddled over, holding it up for everyone to see. Laughter rolled along the shore. Yara grabbed it and wrestled it back on under the water, her face scalding. She stayed crouched in the sea long after she was cold, until the people nearest had packed up and gone.

At the lake Zeb boasted that he could swim to the island and back, and set out with a big splash. Halfway there he ran out of breath and had to be towed back by a lifeguard in front of everyone on the beach, including his new girlfriend's family. They clapped as he was helped out of the water. Zeb stood wrapped in a towel with his head down, his whole face burning, wanting the ground to swallow him. He could not meet anyone's eyes for the rest of the day and sat at the far end of the picnic blanket, silent.
